newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrian unions threaten to turn against euro.
newsitem.headline: Austrian unions threaten to turn against euro.

text.p: Austria's trade unions warned on Friday they would turn against Europe's single currency if the government failed to combat unemployment, delivering a fresh blow to attempts to drum up support for the euro.

"The basic 'Yes' of the Austrian trade union congress (OeGB) to the euro can turn into a 'No'," OeGB chief Franz Verzetnisch said in a newspaper interview, adding the unions would clarify their final position by the end of the year.
"Who will accept the euro if unemployment keeps rising? A euro without jobs -- no thanks," he told Der Standard.

The threat came just a day after the government's chief euro campaigner, Gustav Raab, resigned amid allegations he towed the line of the European Commission, with which he had an agreement to promote its official views on the euro.

According to recent polls, a mere 15 percent of Austrians believe the introduction of the euro will benefit them, while as many as 50 percent are afraid the single currency will hurt the value of their savings.
With unemployment running at record highs in neighbouring Germany, labour issues have taken front seat in Austria's political debate.
The country's unemployment rate inched up to 4.1 percent in March from 3.9 percent a year earlier, but is still among the lowest in the European Union.

"The trade unions are asking for clear measures to boost employment. I am sure there will be talks with them," finance ministry spokesman Andreas Hoeferl told Reuters. "It wouldn't make sense to push through a policy against the unions."
He added Austria had already launched an EU initiative to place greater weight on employment issues. "We'll have to continue on that road," he said.

A proposal by Social Democrat Chancellor Viktor Klima last week to boost employment by cutting both working hours and average pay was greeted with fierce criticism by the unions, traditionally the Social Democrat's closest political allies.

Austria's governing coalition of dominant Social Democrats and the conservative People's Party publicly maintains the country will be among the first group of nations to join Europe's monetary union in 1999.

But the opposition far-right Freedom Party of Joerg Haider has scored substantial electoral gains with its strongly Euro-sceptic views. In European elections last October, the Social Democrat vote slumped to an all-time low, while support for the far right soared to a record 28 percent.

The Freedom Party has urged the government to scrap its campaign for the euro, while the opposition Greens called for a total overhaul of the strategy to make it conform with the "most primitive ground rules of democracy".

Austria joined the European Union and its exchange rate mechanism, the precursor to the single currency, in January 1995 after more than two-thirds of Austrians voted in favour of EU entry in a June 1994 referendum.
